summary:
Lima department and the metropolitan area stand under the national framework of Peru, and the national assessment carried by the parent record applies here. No separate departmental or municipal regime modifying that framework was identified in the sources.

The national norm approved by the legislature's plenary on 2 April 2025 bars entry to and use of public sanitary facilities by any person whose biological sex does not match the sex for which the facility is designated. In Lima, the international airport Jorge Chávez had installed signage reading "for all persons with female identity" and "male identity"; the text also prohibits signage of that kind as "ambiguous", so the inclusive signage already present in the capital's main airport falls within the ban. The Women and Family Commission had approved the fused bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR unanimously on 20 February 2025, at which point the measure still required plenary backing.

LGBTIQ activist Gianna Camacho, quoted by Infobae on 20 February 2025, called the measure discriminatory and described how enforcement would operate in practice: security staff judging for themselves whether a woman entering a restroom is trans, and demanding her national identity document (DNI) on that judgment. The rule therefore converts routine facility use in Lima into a documented-checkpoint risk for gender-nonconforming users.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in analysis of 15 April 2025 by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, characterises article 5 of the text as direct legislation conditioning basic rights on a "biological sex", a violation of the equality and non-discrimination principle. The authors note that trans people, though framed in the debate as aggressors, are more often the victims of violence and discrimination.

Recorded violence against LGBTI people in Peru, in counts that include Lima, is substantial and rising: the TLGBI Rights Observatory annual report recorded 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reports of rights violations between 2020 and 2023. More than half of those killed were trans women (30), followed by 23 gay men and one lesbian. The year 2023 saw the most homicides (19), and no suspects were identified in 26 of the 54 killings. These are raw counts on a national denominator that includes Lima; the source provides no per-capita or city-level breakdown, so the figures cannot be read as a Lima-specific rate.

One of those killings occurred in central Lima: on 12 February 2023 the transgender sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, aged 31, was kidnapped from jirón Chancay by the "Los Gallegos" extortion gang and killed with roughly 30 gunshots. Agencia Presentes, reporting on 22 July 2024, flags the state inaction around such cases: no official system records victims' sexual orientation, and hate crimes go unsanctioned.
tangentialFactors:
The observatory figures are compiled by a civil-society body precisely because the state maintains no official register of victims' sexual orientation or gender identity. The absence of a state data system is itself the reason the only available counts are non-official, and it means the raw totals are a floor rather than a measurement.

The legislative debate inverts the evidentiary record: trans people are presented in the chamber as a risk to be screened out of restrooms, while the same period's documentation shows them as the largest single group of those killed. The IDEHPUCP analysis makes that inversion explicit, and the enforcement mechanism described by Gianna Camacho — staff deciding who "looks trans" and demanding identity papers — places the burden of that framing on gender-nonconforming people in everyday transit spaces, including the capital's airport.

The inclusive signage at Jorge Chávez airport indicates that identity-respecting facility practice already existed in Lima before the national norm prohibited signage of that kind, so the change is a withdrawal of an operating arrangement rather than the introduction of a new one.
localsOnly:
Residents of Lima who are trans or gender-nonconforming face identity-document checks by security staff whenever they use public restrooms, since enforcement of the national norm rests on staff's own assessment of whether a user's appearance matches the designated facility. Carrying a DNI does not resolve the encounter, because the trigger is the staff member's judgment rather than a document discrepancy.

Hate-crime reporting for residents has no official channel of record: the state does not maintain a system capturing victims' sexual orientation or gender identity, so documented cases depend on the TLGBI Rights Observatory and similar civil-society collection. Residents pursuing accountability therefore enter a process in which the underlying pattern is unrecorded by the authorities and, per Agencia Presentes, hate crimes go unsanctioned.

The 2020–2023 observatory totals (54 killings, 170 reports of rights violations, with 30 of the dead trans women and no suspects identified in 26 killings) are the working evidence base for advocacy in Lima, since no state equivalent exists.
outOfScopeNotes:
The observatory counts are national totals that include Lima; no Lima-only breakdown of killings or reports is sourced, and no per-capita denominator is provided, so the relative exposure of a resident of Lima compared with other parts of Peru remains unresolved.

The outcome of the criminal case over the killing of Rubí Torres Silvano on 12 February 2023, including whether any suspects were identified or charged, is not sourced here.

Whether Jorge Chávez airport altered or removed its inclusive signage after the national norm was approved is not sourced.

Whether Lima's regional or municipal authorities issued implementing guidance, signage directives or enforcement protocols for the public-facility rule is not sourced, nor is whether the norm has been challenged before Lima courts.

Whether the 170 recorded reports of rights violations include incidents at Lima facilities or transit spaces specifically is not sourced.
